intelliGen iF/iRC controller: Which machines show this code: The intelliGen refrigeration controller is Heatcraft's current-generation control system, factory-fitted to unit coolers sold under Heatcraft's brands — Bohn and Larkin most commonly, along with Climate Control and Chandler. If your walk-in's evaporator carries one of those nameplates and shows a small OLED text display with a colored light bar, this is your controller. It reports with AL (alarm), ER (error), and IN (information) codes on the display, backed by the light bar: green is normal, yellow is a non-critical fault, red means act now. On newer A2L-refrigerant unit coolers it also runs the built-in refrigerant leak detection system. Practical tip: photograph the display before power-cycling — the code and light bar color together tell the technician most of the story.
Beacon II refrigeration system: Which machines show this code: Beacon II is Heatcraft's previous-generation smart refrigeration system, shipped for years on walk-in evaporators and condensing units branded Bohn and Larkin (plus Climate Control and Chandler). Huge numbers of these are still running in restaurants and stores, so these codes come up constantly on older boxes. The evaporator control board reports through a simple two-digit readout: A-codes (A1–A4) are alarms about box conditions, E-codes (E1–E9) are equipment faults like failed sensors or tripped compressor safeties. On multi-evaporator installs, which board shows the code tells you where the problem is. Practical tip: write down the exact code and whether the compressor is running before resetting anything — several Beacon II faults pump the system down and keep it off until repaired.
Beacon II Smart Controller (LCD display: Which machines show this code: The Beacon II Smart Controller is the optional wall-mounted LCD display that ties into Beacon II evaporator boards on Bohn and Larkin walk-in systems, letting staff monitor several coolers and freezers from one panel outside the box. Instead of two-digit codes it shows scrolling text messages — like *BOXHI or *INFLT with "CALL FOR SERVICE" — plus the system number affected, and sounds a buzzer. Remember it is a messenger: the fault it reports lives at the evaporator board or refrigeration system it monitors, not in the display itself. Practical tip: press CLEAR to silence the buzzer, but write down the message and system number first — that pairing tells the technician exactly which unit to walk to.
KE2 Evaporator Efficiency: Which machines show this code: The KE2 Evaporator Efficiency (KE2 Evap) from KE2 Therm is an aftermarket and OEM evaporator controller found on walk-in coolers and freezers of nearly any box brand — it's one of the most common retrofit controls in the country, often installed to add demand defrost and remote monitoring to an existing walk-in. If your evaporator has a small KE2 display that scrolls text alarms in plain words (HIGH AIR TEMP, DOOR SWITCH, EXCESS DEFROST) rather than cryptic codes, this is it. A yellow LED means a non-critical alarm with the system still running; a red LED is critical. Practical tip: the VARIABLES menu shows live sensor readings — a temperature of -87 means an unplugged sensor, 180+ means a shorted one.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX): Which machines show this code: Dixell's XR series (now under Emerson/Copeland) is probably the most widely installed walk-in thermostat family there is. The small panel-mount XR06CX and XR60CX ship as the standard controller on boxes from Norlake, Kolpak, and many other walk-in manufacturers, and they're a favorite replacement control when an original thermostat dies. The display normally shows box temperature; when something's wrong, a short two- or three-character code flashes or alternates with the temperature — P-codes for failed probes, HA/LA for temperature alarms, dA for the door, CA for a shutdown-level fault. Practical tip: most alarms silence when you press any key but keep displaying until the condition clears — so a code still showing means the problem is still live.
XR-series (XR60CX): Which machines show this code: These codes are specific to the Dixell XR60CX, the bigger sibling in the XR series (Emerson/Copeland) with defrost, fan control, and support for up to four probes. Like the rest of the XR family it ships on walk-in boxes from Norlake, Kolpak, and many other manufacturers, and is a common field replacement controller. The extra probes are what create these codes: P3 and P4 flag the optional third and fourth probes, while HA2 and LA2 are condenser-temperature alarms that only exist when a condenser probe is fitted. Refrigeration usually continues while these show. Practical tip: HA2 is the controller telling you the condenser is running hot — nine times out of ten that's a dirty coil or blocked airflow you can see with your own eyes.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas: Which machines show this code: This is Norlake's programmable walk-in controller — a control panel built on the Carel PCO5+ platform, supplied with Norlake walk-in coolers and freezers and their refrigeration packages. Unlike the tiny code-flashing thermostats on many boxes, this one has a multi-line LCD that spells alarms out in full English — DOOR AJAR ALARM, ROOM TEMP HIGH ALARM, AIR FLOW LOSS — with an ALARM button that silences the buzzer and steps through active alarms. The status line on MENU 1 also tells you when the controller is running on a backup sensor. Practical tip: pressing ALARM after closing a left-open door doesn't just silence the noise — it deliberately delays the air-temperature alarm to give the room time to recover, which is exactly what Norlake intends you to do.
ERC 211/213/214: Which machines show this code: The Danfoss ERC 211, 213, and 214 are compact electronic refrigeration controllers fitted by many commercial cabinet and refrigeration equipment makers, and they turn up on walk-in panels as well as reach-ins and display cases. The display normally shows temperature; faults appear as E-codes for failed sensors (E27 defrost, E29 air, E30 condenser) and A-codes for alarm conditions — temperature, voltage, condenser, and door alarms. One code worth knowing before you panic: A45 means the unit was switched to standby on purpose via its main-switch parameter, not that anything broke. Practical tip: A80 (condenser blocked) is manual-reset — clean the coil first, then power-cycle, or it just comes straight back.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210: Which machines show this code: The Danfoss EKC 202 and its successor the AK-CC 210 are panel-mount case controllers used across commercial refrigeration — display cases, cold rooms, and walk-in evaporator control, often tied into a store's front-end monitoring network. Faults show as short codes plus a plain-text line on the display: E-codes are defects (E1 controller fault, E27 and E29 sensor errors) and A-codes are alarms (A1 high temperature, A2 low, A4 door, A45 standby). Practical tip: A45 standby doesn't trip the alarm relay on the AK-CC 210 — a box someone left in standby can sit warming quietly, so treat an unexplained 'Standby mode' display as urgent, not informational.
AK-CC 210/250: Which machines show this code: The Danfoss AK-CC 210 and AK-CC 250 are case controllers for commercial refrigeration — cold rooms, display cases, and walk-in evaporator sections, frequently networked into a central monitoring system that logs their alarms. They report with the same short-code convention as the rest of Danfoss's EKC/AK line: E-codes for sensor and hardware defects (E25 and E26 are the S3 and S4 air sensors) and A-codes for alarm conditions, including A60, a dedicated HACCP high-temperature alarm for food-safety monitoring. Practical tip: when A60 shows, log the actual product temperature immediately — that alarm is a compliance record as much as an equipment warning, and your notes matter at inspection time.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller: Which machines show this code: Danfoss Optyma Plus condensing units — the outdoor or machine-room half of many walk-in cooler and freezer installations — carry their own built-in electronic controller with a small display on the unit. It reports faults as short codes: A-codes for alarms (A2 low suction pressure, A17 pressure safety trip, A80 condenser airflow, A96 discharge temperature) and E-codes for controller defects. Because this controller lives on the condensing unit, its alarms lean toward compressor protection — pressure trips and overheating — rather than box temperature. Practical tip: when one of these codes stops the compressor, resist the urge to keep resetting; the protections exist because forcing restarts is how compressors get destroyed.
ir33 / ir33+: Which machines show this code: The Carel ir33 and ir33+ are among the most widely used electronic refrigeration controllers in the world, fitted by walk-in box and case OEMs and installed by contractors as replacement controls on coolers and freezers of every brand. The display normally shows temperature; a fault alternates a short code with the reading — E-codes for probe failures, HI/LO for temperature alarms, dor for the door, cht/CHt for the condenser, HA/HF for HACCP excursion logs. Practical tip: lowercase and uppercase matter — cht is an early dirty-condenser warning you can act on with a coil cleaning, while CHt is the escalated manual-reset alarm that means the warning stage was missed.
PJ Easy (PJEZ): Which machines show this code: The Carel PJ Easy (PJEZ) is a small, low-cost panel-mount controller that box and case OEMs fit widely to coolers, freezers, and walk-in panels, and that contractors commonly install as a replacement thermostat. It uses short two- or three-character codes that alternate with the temperature reading: E0/E1/E2 for failed probes, HI/LO for temperature alarms, dOR (shown as 'dr' on some models) for the door, cht/CHt for a dirty condenser, EE/EF for parameter memory errors. Practical tip: dF flashing on the display just means a defrost is running — it's normal status, not a fault, so wait out the cycle before assuming something is wrong.
